transcript: In 1994, there was a really big earthquake. And I was young, but I I remember it. I remember it so much. And after that, personally, like I've always been really afraid of earthquakes. And they've been telling us the big one's coming. The big one's coming. And it's like, okay, great. But like, give me solutions here. Growing up, the big one was described as like it's going to be this insane earthquake that's going to like split California in half. Pangia, you know, a a new continent's going to start. Like, it's going to be chaos. The Golden Gate Bridge is gonna freaking just like everything is just going to be over. And again, I'm like, "Okay, great. So, is do I need a flashlight, you know, running shoes, like what what do I need here?" So, there is like some some facts behind this. Okay. Scientists believe that this big one uh will happen along the San Andreas fault in California. The San Andreas is one of the longest faults in the whole world. Not a great movie though. San Andreas. Did you like it? I didn't like it. That was kind of lame, but whatever. Now, here's the fun part that I think just keeps us on our toes. They keep telling us, you know, it's the big one's coming. The big one's coming. We're like, when? and they're like sometime soon or not. And it's like, okay, cool. Faults. What's a fault? Sometimes it's his fault. Sometimes it's her fault. Sometimes, I mean, it's California's fault. The San Andreas fault is the place in California where two tectonic plates meet. Remember plates? So, two of them are meeting. The Pacific plate and the North American plate. Yeah, the plates all have names, too, but we don't need to get too much into that. So, they meet here, but instead of fitting perfectly together, they slide past each other. Now, sometimes when they're slipping and they're sliding, they get stuck. And when they finally unstick, the ground shakes and that's when the earthquake happens. So, the San Andreas fault is like a crack in the earth where big pieces are just trying to move and groove, but they don't always get along nicely. Over the last 1,000 years, there has been at least one major earthquake on the San Andreas fault about every 150 years. And by major earthquake meaning it's bigger than uh 7.0. But the scientists have been doing the math and they're realizing that a big earthquake hasn't hit the area in over 160 years. Great. I'm going to sleep so well tonight. Thanks. You know, thanks Bailey for ruining my day. So, technically, according to scientists and everyone who's who studies earthquakes, they're like, "Yeah, we're overdue. It's going to happen. We just don't know when." Look, maybe it won't happen in our lifetime and then I'll be dead. So, I won't it won't matter, but good luck to everyone else in the future, you know?
